title: Exodus
subtitle: Out of Egypt, to the mountain, into God's tent
lead: Exodus, from the Greek for "going out," is called in Hebrew Shemot, "Names," after its opening words: "These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt." It tells how a family became a people. Chapters 1–15 tell of slavery in Egypt, the call of Moses at the burning bush, the revealing of God's name, ten blows on Egypt, the first Passover and the crossing of the Sea of Reeds, ending in the Song of the Sea. Chapters 16–24 lead through the wilderness to Mount Sinai, where God gives the Ten Words and a covenant. Chapters 25–40 describe the tabernacle, the tent where God will live among his people, broken off by the golden calf and resumed until the glory of the LORD fills the tent.

The book's movement is from serving Pharaoh to serving God: the same Hebrew word, avad, means both slavery and worship. Its question is Pharaoh's: "Who is this LORD?" (5:2). Its answer is a name, "I will be who I will be" (3:14), shown in acts of rescue and spelled out at the mountain: "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love" (34:6).

Exodus has shaped more than religion. It is the story of the Jewish Passover and of the Christian Easter, and it has been read as the founding charter of freedom movements from the Puritans to the spirituals of enslaved Africans and the speeches of Martin Luther King Jr. Its history is fiercely debated: some date the exodus about 1446 BC, others in the 1200s BC, and many scholars find no trace of a mass exodus at all. This edition sets out each view at its strongest and lets the reader weigh them.
facts: Not named. Jewish and Christian tradition: Moses. Most critical scholars: several sources woven together, finished during or after the exile.
Set in the 1400s or 1200s BC (scholars and traditions differ). Most critical scholars: written from the 900s to the 400s BC, with some old poetry (15:1–18) perhaps from the 1100s BC.
Egypt, the Sinai wilderness, and Mount Sinai
Story, poetry (the Song of the Sea), law, and building instructions

audience.to: The people of Israel, told how they became a people. On the traditional view the first hearers were the generation that came out of Egypt and stood at Mount Sinai, and their children who were about to enter Canaan. They were former slaves who had to learn to live as a free people under God's covenant. On the critical view older parts were told and sung in Israel and Judah under the kings: the Song of the Sea, the Covenant Code, and stories of Moses. The finished book was then shaped for Judeans during and after the exile to Babylon. They had lost their Temple and were rebuilding a life of worship under Persian rule.
audience.why: To tell Israel how the LORD freed them from Pharaoh to serve him instead. He bound them to himself by covenant and law at Sinai, forgave them after the golden calf, and came to live among them in the tabernacle. The book answers Pharaoh's question, "Who is this LORD?" (5:2). Knowing the audience changes the reading. The Passover rules speak to households in the land who will tell their children what the rite means (12:24–27; 13:14). The Covenant Code is written for farmers in villages with fields, vineyards, oxen and local courts, not for slaves in Egypt. The golden calf, so close to the calves of Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28), warned the kingdoms. The long plans for God's dwelling taught a people who had a temple, or had lost one, how a holy God can live with a sinful people. On the chapter pages, "First for" names the people inside the story, and "For the book's readers" says what the words meant to Israel hearing it.
views: Moses, for the people at Sinai

Jewish and Christian tradition holds that Moses wrote Exodus, as the book says he wrote down the covenant (24:4) and the renewed covenant (34:27). It was for the Israelites of the wilderness and their children who would enter the land.

Many conservative scholars (Kitchen, Hoffmeier, Stuart) hold that the book comes from Moses' time or soon after, with its Egyptian details. Later scribes updated names and added notes for readers already in the land (16:35; 40:36–38).

The Documentary Hypothesis is the theory that the Torah was woven from older written sources. On this view the Yahwist (J) and Elohist (E) stories of Moses were told in Judah and Israel under the kings. Many date the Covenant Code to early Israel or the time of the kings. The Song of the Sea may be among the oldest poems in the Bible.
A Priestly source from before the exile

Yehezkel Kaufmann, Menahem Haran and Jacob Milgrom date the Priestly source (P), which includes the tabernacle chapters, before the exile. Avi Hurvitz supports this from the Hebrew of P. Haran sees in the tabernacle a picture of the First Temple of Jerusalem, and links P's rules to King Hezekiah's reforms (about 700 BC).
A Priestly book for exiles and returnees

Many critical scholars date P and the final book to the exile or the Persian period. Then the tabernacle served as a model for the Second Temple, and the Sabbath as a sign of belonging. Some (Schmid) think the exodus was once a separate origin story, joined to the stories of the fathers only then.

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional Jewish and Christian reading, defended today by scholars such as Kitchen and Hoffmeier: a nation of Israelites left Egypt under Moses, with signs and wonders, in the 1400s or 1200s BC.

lenses.name: Historical core
lenses.desc: Many scholars (for example Richard Friedman and William Dever's 'Exodus group') think a smaller group, perhaps the Levites, came out of Egypt, and their story became all Israel's story.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most academic scholars find no evidence of a mass exodus and read the book as Israel's founding memory, built from older traditions and sources and shaped in the age of the kings and the exile.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The Passover Haggadah, the Midrash (Mekhilta, Exodus Rabbah), Rashi, Ramban and later thinkers read Exodus as the birth of the Jewish people, the giving of the Torah, and God's presence living among them.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: The church reads the exodus as a pattern of salvation fulfilled in Christ: the Passover lamb, the sea as baptism, manna as the bread of life, the tabernacle as God dwelling among us (John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 5:7; 10:1–4).

Plain English Translation

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level, written from the Hebrew word by word rather than adapted from another English version. YHWH is "the LORD" and Adonai is "Lord." God's answer in 3:14 is "I will be who I will be," with "I Will Be" as its short form, and El Shaddai is "God Almighty." The three verbs used of Pharaoh's heart are kept apart: "stubborn" (chazaq), "heavy" (kaved) and "hard" (qashah). Yam Suf is "Sea of Reeds," not "Red Sea." The verb avad is "serve" both for slavery and for worship, to keep the book's wordplay. Chesed is "loyal love" throughout, ga'al "redeem" and padah "ransom." The Ten Commandments are called "the Ten Words," as the book names them (34:28), and the lid of the ark is the "atonement lid." Poetry, such as the Song of the Sea, is set in lines divided by " / ". Verse numbers follow English Bibles. They differ from the Hebrew in chapter 8 (English 8:1–4 are Hebrew 7:26–29, so every later verse of chapter 8 is four higher in English) and in chapter 22 (English 22:1 is Hebrew 21:37, so English 22:2–31 are Hebrew 22:1–30).

Where the Masoretic Text differs from the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint or the Dead Sea Scrolls in a way that matters, the variant is shown beside the verse: for example the seventy or seventy-five descendants of Jacob (1:5), the 430 years "in Egypt" or "in Egypt and Canaan" (12:40, Septuagint and Samaritan), and the chariot wheels "removed" or "clogged" (14:25).

KJV, ASV, WEB, YLT

Public-domain English versions. The KJV (1611, standard text of 1769) prints words the translators added in italics. Young's Literal Translation (1898) keeps Hebrew word order and tenses.

BSB

The Berean Standard Bible, a modern translation released into the public domain.

Hebrew

The Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008), as edited by the Westminster Leningrad Codex project and corrected in STEPBible's TAHOT (Tyndale House, Cambridge), with each word's meaning and grammar.

Exodus is three books in one: a story of rescue (1–18), a covenant with its laws (19–24), and a building project (25–40), with the golden calf (32–34) as the crisis in the middle of the last. The parts belong together. Rescue leads to covenant, covenant to the tabernacle, and the tabernacle to God's presence: the book begins with Israel in Pharaoh's house and ends with God in Israel's tent (40:34).

Watch for key words. Israel "serves" Pharaoh until it can "serve" God. The LORD acts so that Egypt and Israel "will know that I am the LORD." Pharaoh's heart is "heavy," and God wins "glory," kavod, from the same root, a glory that at last fills the tabernacle. Water runs through the story: the Nile that drowns sons and saves Moses, the river turned to blood, the sea split, bitter water made sweet, and water from the rock.

No Egyptian text mentions Israel's slavery, Moses or the plagues, and the absence is read in opposite ways. Traditional scholars note that Egyptian records rarely record defeats, that a population of Semites lived in the eastern Delta for centuries, and that details of the story fit New Kingdom Egypt: the store city Pi-Ramesses, brick quotas, Egyptian names among the Levites (Moses, Phinehas, Hophni), the border forts of the Ways of Horus. The Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) shows that a people Israel lived in Canaan by then. They date the exodus either about 1446 BC, following 1 Kings 6:1, or in the 1260s BC, following the name Rameses.

A middle view, held by Richard Friedman, William Dever (for an "Exodus group") and others, is that a smaller group, perhaps the Levites, came out of Egypt, and their memory became all Israel's story. Critical scholars such as Israel Finkelstein point to the lack of any trace of two million people in Sinai and to Israel's emergence from within Canaan, and read the exodus as a founding memory shaped in the age of the kings, perhaps recalling the expulsion of the Hyksos (about 1550 BC) and Egypt's long rule over Canaan. Each chapter page sets out these views, using the lenses H, M and C.

Exodus is central to source criticism. The name of God is revealed twice, in 3:14–15 and 6:2–3, and 6:3 says the patriarchs did not know the name YHWH, although Genesis uses it from 4:26 on. Many plagues and the sea crossing contain doubled features: a wind drives the sea back all night (14:21a), and the waters split at Moses' raised hand to stand as walls (14:21b–22). The tabernacle chapters (25–31; 35–40) share the language and concerns of Leviticus. Most critical scholars assign these to different sources (J, E and P, or a Priestly and a non-Priestly strand), while conservative scholars read the repetitions as deliberate narrative technique, as in other ancient Near Eastern literature (Umberto Cassuto, Kenneth Kitchen).

For Judaism, Exodus is the birth of the people and the giving of the Torah. The exodus is remembered daily: in the Shema's third paragraph, in the whole Song of the Sea (Az Yashir, 15:1–18) recited each morning in Pesukei de-Zimra, in Mi khamokha (15:11) and 15:18 in the blessing after the Shema morning and evening, and in the Kiddush that calls the Sabbath "a remembrance of the exodus." Passover re-enacts chapters 12–13 at the Seder table through the Haggadah, and the festival of Shavuot recalls Sinai. The Mekhilta of Rabbi Ishmael is the classic early commentary on chapters 12–23; Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban and Rashbam are the great medieval readers.

sections.b: The New Testament reads the exodus as a pattern of salvation. At the transfiguration Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus of the exodos he will complete at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Jesus' death falls at Passover, and he is "our Passover" (1 Corinthians 5:7); the sea is a baptism and the rock is Christ (1 Corinthians 10:1–4); the manna points to the bread from heaven (John 6:31–35); the Word "pitched his tent" among us as the tabernacle did (John 1:14), and Hebrews reads the priesthood and tabernacle as shadows of Christ's work (Hebrews 8–10). The church fathers developed this into full typology (Melito of Sardis, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Moses). Exodus has also been central to liberation theology, Black theology and the American civil rights movement, while some Christian readers have questioned its violence and its use to justify conquest (Robert Warrior).

sections.b: Exodus is well preserved. Fragments of roughly fifteen to eighteen scrolls of Exodus were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. The most important, 4QpaleoExod-m, written in the old Hebrew script, shares with the Samaritan Pentateuch long expansions of the plague stories, in which each command to Moses is followed by a full report of its delivery to Pharaoh. The Septuagint of Exodus is a free and skilled translation; its tabernacle chapters (35–40) differ notably from the Hebrew in order and content, which may point to a different edition of those chapters. Smaller differences include the number of Jacob's descendants (1:5), where the scrolls 4QGen-Exod-a and 4QExod-b side with the Septuagint's seventy-five against the Masoretic seventy, so the scrolls do not simply support the standard Hebrew, and the length of Israel's stay (12:40).

reading: William H. C. Propp, Exodus 1–18 and Exodus 19–40 (Anchor Bible, 1999, 2006)
The fullest critical commentary, strong on the Hebrew text, the versions and ancient Near Eastern background.
Brevard S. Childs, The Book of Exodus (Old Testament Library, 1974)
A landmark commentary that combines source criticism, the history of interpretation and theology.
Nahum M. Sarna, Exodus (JPS Torah Commentary, 1991) and Exploring Exodus (1986)
Compact Jewish commentary and a readable study of the book's history and ideas.
Umberto Cassuto, A Commentary on the Book of Exodus (1967)
A Jewish scholar's close literary reading that argues against splitting the text into sources.
Carol Meyers, Exodus (New Cambridge Bible Commentary, 2005)
A clear critical commentary attentive to archaeology, social history and women.
Terence E. Fretheim, Exodus (Interpretation, 1991)
A theological commentary that reads the plagues and the tabernacle through the lens of creation.
Douglas K. Stuart, Exodus (New American Commentary, 2006)
A detailed evangelical commentary defending the book's historical reliability.
James K. Hoffmeier, Israel in Egypt (1997) and Ancient Israel in Sinai (2005)
An Egyptologist's case for the authenticity of the exodus and wilderness traditions.
Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman, The Bible Unearthed (2001)
The most widely read critical account of the archaeology, arguing against a historical mass exodus.
Richard Elliott Friedman, The Exodus (2017)
Argues that a smaller group, the Levites, really came out of Egypt.
Michael Walzer, Exodus and Revolution (1985)
How the exodus became the West's model for political liberation.
Gregory of Nyssa, The Life of Moses (about AD 390)
The classic early Christian spiritual reading of Moses' life as the soul's ascent to God.

spec.title: Exodus as a book about who Israel serves
spec.body: My own reading of the whole book: Exodus turns on one Hebrew verb, avad, "serve, work, worship." Israel begins as Pharaoh's slaves doing "every kind of labor" (1:14); Moses demands "Let my people go, so they may serve me"; Pharaoh's officials cry "we let Israel go, and now they no longer serve us" (14:5); and the book ends with Israel doing the "work" (avodah) of the tabernacle, exactly as commanded (39:42). The building chapters, often found dull, are the answer to the brick quotas of chapters 1 and 5: labor given freely, "every person whose heart lifted him" (35:21), with more than enough (36:5–7). Freedom in Exodus is not the absence of service but the exchange of a master. Terence Fretheim and others have made a similar case; my own addition is the link between the building chapters and the brick quotas. This is a reading, not a proof, but the vocabulary supports it.

spec.title: Why the exodus memory might be both true and enlarged
spec.body: A speculation that tries to honor both the H and C lenses: the strongest evidence for some real departure from Egypt is the kind of detail that later inventors would not choose, such as an Egyptian name for the founder and Egyptian names among the priests, while the strongest evidence against a nation of two million is the silence of Sinai's archaeology. A memory carried by a smaller group, then told and sung by a whole people as their own ("what the LORD did for me," 13:8), would produce exactly what we have: Egyptian color, numbers that grew, and a liturgy that invites every later generation into the story. I hold this loosely; it is one of the M-lens views in my own words.

authorship: Jewish and Christian tradition holds that Moses wrote the Torah (Talmud, Bava Batra 14b; Philo; Josephus). Exodus itself says Moses wrote down particular texts: the war against Amalek (17:14), "all the words of the LORD" in the Book of the Covenant (24:4, 7), and the words of the renewed covenant (34:27). Jesus speaks of "the book of Moses" when quoting the bush scene (Mark 12:26). The question is old: the medieval commentator Ibn Ezra hinted (his "secret of the twelve") that a few lines of the Torah were added after Moses. Defenders point to the book's knowledge of Egypt: Egyptian names, brickmaking, the Nile, the chariot army and the seasons of flax and barley (9:31).

Many conservative scholars (for example Kenneth Kitchen, James Hoffmeier, Douglas Stuart) hold that Exodus is substantially from Moses' time or soon after, using records, songs and laws of that age, with later scribes updating names such as "Rameses" (1:11) and "the Philistines' land" (13:17) and adding notes such as the closing summaries of the wilderness journey (40:36–38).

Since Jean Astruc (1753) and Julius Wellhausen (1878), most critical scholars have found several sources: J (using YHWH from the start), E (using "God" until 3:14), and P (the Priestly source, in which the name YHWH is first revealed in 6:3), combined by later editors. The two call stories (3–4; 6:2–7:7), the doubled plague and sea accounts, and the tabernacle chapters (P) are central evidence. Richard Elliott Friedman and Joel Baden represent the classic and newer forms of this view.

Many European scholars now doubt a continuous J and E. They see a Priestly composition and a non-Priestly story of Moses and the exodus that once circulated separately from the stories of the patriarchs, joined to Genesis only in the Persian period (for example Konrad Schmid and Thomas Dozeman). On this view the exodus was one of Israel's two rival origin stories, the other being descent from Jacob.
